newsitem.title: UK: Labour must show positive EMU approach say bankers.
newsitem.headline: Labour must show positive EMU approach say bankers.

text.p: A positive approach by Britain's new Labour government to European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) will help London-based international investment banks to develop, said an industry report on Friday.

"If the newly-elected government does not convince business interests that the option to join EMU by 2002, is genuine, then commercial plans will be based on a prospect of indefinite non-participation," the London Investment Bankers Association (LIBA) said in a report.
But a positive approach could assist its members "to participate fully in the development of the wholesale euro-financial markets, building on London's competitive edge", it added.
Earlier Britain's Labour party won a landslide election victory, ousting the ruling Conservatives.
LIBA said City-based financial firms had a strong commercial interest in encouraging the development of an efficient infrastructure and regulatory regime for euro-denominated business in London.
The trade association said this would require action from the new Labour government in key areas.

It will have to provide parliamentary and regulatory action such as bringing proposed regulations on the legal basis of the single currency quickly before parliament to give markets legal certainty, LIBA said.

Labour will also have to begin serious planning to "maintain the option of completing the conversion by 2002" and send sufficient signals to the British private sector and other European Union member states that the option of joining was a credible policy.
"Every aspect of the government's approach will send a subtle, but powerful, signal about long run intentions," it said.

The association detailed technical recommendations "to ease the transition process and lay the foundations for a large, simple and transparent financial market denominated in euros, where London-based banks can play a major role".

These cover the need for legal certainty in the EU and beyond, the mechanics of allowing bond and equity markets to convert to the single currency whether Britain was involved or not, the operations of the European Central Bank and the pace of preparations in securities settlements.
LIBA said this last area was one where "there is already a risk of disruption to markets".

Its progress report on the transition to euro capital markets resulted from the establishment in June 1995 of a LIBA EMU committee. This has members from a wide range of investment banks in the City of London and has produced three reports.

LIBA said it did not to seek to focus on whether Britain should join up to the single currency but on the requirements imposed on its members. Labour has adopted a "wait and see" approach on whether Britain should join the first wave of the euro in 1999.
"In 422 business days, a significant part of LIBA members' activities will be converted to euro. A smooth, successful transition is a key business issue to our members," it said.
